subject: maths
title: Primary 3 Area and Perimeter
seo_title: P3 Area and Perimeter Worksheets: Free Primary 3 Maths with Answers (MOE Syllabus)
standard_text: Concepts of area and perimeter; area in square units, cm² and m²; perimeter of rectilinear figures, rectangles and squares; area of rectangles and squares
meta_desc: Free P3 maths practice: count squares for area, find perimeters, area of rectangles in cm² and m², rectilinear figures. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Area is the surface inside (cm², m²). Perimeter is the distance round (cm, m).
key_sub: A rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm: area = 8 × 5 = 40 cm², perimeter = 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 cm.
body_html:
Area: count the squares

Area is the amount of surface a figure covers. We measure it in squares. If each square is 1 square unit, count the squares inside. Squares of 1 cm by 1 cm give the area in square centimetres (cm²). Big spaces like a floor are measured in square metres (m²).

Perimeter: the distance round

Perimeter is the total length of the sides all the way round a figure. On a grid, count the sides of the small squares along the thick green line, not the squares. Perimeter is a length, so it is in cm or m.

For the same rectangle: 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm. A corner square has 2 sides on the edge, so count both sides.

Rectangles and squares

Area of a rectangle = length × breadth. Perimeter of a rectangle = add all 4 sides (length + breadth + length + breadth). A square has 4 equal sides.

Example

A square has sides of 6 m. Find its area and its perimeter.

Area: 6 × 6 = 36 m². Perimeter: 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24 m.

Answer: 36 m² and 24 m

Perimeter of a rectilinear figure

A rectilinear figure has only straight sides that meet at right angles. Find any side with no label first, then add all the sides.

Area or perimeter?

Tiles, carpet and paint cover a surface: find the area. A fence, a border or a ribbon goes round the edge: find the perimeter.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Adding the sides for the area (8 + 5 = 13)Multiply: 8 × 5 = 40 cm²
Multiplying for the perimeter (8 × 5 = 40)Add all 4 sides: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 cm
Adding only 2 sides of a rectangle (8 + 5)A rectangle has 4 sides
Counting the squares round the edge for the perimeter (12)Count the sides of the squares (16)
Counting the corner squares twice for a border of tilesCount each square only once
Writing cm for an area, or cm² for a perimeterArea: cm² or m². Perimeter: cm or m

faq.q: What is taught in P3 area and perimeter?
faq.a: Primary 3 students find area by counting squares in square units, cm² and m², find the area of rectangles and squares, and find the perimeter of rectangles, squares and rectilinear figures.

faq.q: How do I explain the difference between area and perimeter to my child?
faq.a: Area is the surface a shape covers, like the tiles on a floor. Perimeter is the distance round the edge, like a fence round a garden.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake in area and perimeter?
faq.a: Mixing them up: adding the sides when the question asks for area, or multiplying when it asks for perimeter. Writing cm for an area instead of cm² is another common slip.

faq.q: Is area and perimeter in the MOE Primary 3 syllabus?
faq.a: Yes. It is in Measurement and Geometry (Area and Volume) of the MOE 2021 Primary Mathematics Syllabus. Primary 4 then moves on to composite figures made of rectangles and squares.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded frame?
items.e: Count each square once. Top and bottom rows: 5 + 5 = 10. The sides have 2 + 2 more (the corner squares are already counted). 10 + 4 = 14 cm². (18 cm² counts the 4 corner squares twice.)

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded rectangle?
items.e: Count the squares inside: 2 rows of 6 squares. 2 × 6 = 12, so the area is 12 cm². (16 is the perimeter, the distance round the edge.)

items.q: A rectangle is covered with 3 rows of 1 cm² squares. There are 7 squares in each row. What is its area?
items.e: 3 rows of 7 squares: 3 × 7 = 21 squares, so the area is 21 cm².

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded figure?
items.e: Count the shaded squares one by one, and tick each one so you count it only once: 11 squares. The area is 11 cm². (Do not count the empty squares that make it a full rectangle.)

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded rectangle?

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × breadth = 9 × 7 = 63 m². (32 m is the perimeter.)

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × breadth = 8 × 6 = 48 cm². (28 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: A rectangle has a length of 12 cm and a breadth of 5 cm. What is its area?
items.e: Area = length × breadth = 12 × 5. 10 × 5 = 50 and 2 × 5 = 10. 50 + 10 = 60 cm².

items.q: The area of this rectangle is 45 m². What is the length of the side marked ?
items.e: Length × breadth = area, so 9 × ? = 45. 45 ÷ 9 = 5 m. Check: 9 × 5 = 45.

items.q: The area of this rectangle is 24 cm². What is the length of the side marked ?
items.e: Length × breadth = area, so 6 × ? = 24. 24 ÷ 6 = 4 cm. Check: 6 × 4 = 24.

items.e: Area = length × breadth = 5 × 3 = 15 cm². (16 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × breadth = 9 × 6 = 54 cm². (30 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: Which unit is best for the area of a postage stamp?
items.e: A stamp is small, and area is the surface it covers, so use square centimetres. cm and m measure length; cm² and m² measure area.

items.q: Which unit is best for the area of a classroom floor?
items.e: A floor is big, and area is the surface it covers, so use square metres. cm and m measure length; cm² and m² measure area.

items.q: This is a square. What is its area?
items.e: All sides of a square are equal, so the length and the breadth are both 5 cm. 5 × 5 = 25 cm². (20 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × breadth = 6 × 2 = 12 m². (16 m is the perimeter.)

items.q: Which unit is best for the length of a pencil?
items.e: Length is not an area. A pencil is short, so use centimetres. cm and m measure length; cm² and m² measure area.

items.q: This is a square. What is its area?
items.e: All sides of a square are equal, so the length and the breadth are both 8 m. 8 × 8 = 64 m². (32 m is the perimeter.)

items.q: Rectangle A is 6 cm long and 4 cm wide. Square B has sides of 5 cm. Which has the bigger area?
items.e: A: 6 × 4 = 24 cm². B: 5 × 5 = 25 cm². 25 − 24 = 1, so B is bigger by 1 cm². (Their perimeters are both 20 cm, but the areas are different.)

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × breadth = 8 × 4 = 32 m². (24 m is the perimeter.)

items.q: A rectangle has a length of 20 m and a breadth of 3 m. What is its area?
items.e: Area = length × breadth = 20 × 3 = 60 m².

items.q: A rectangle has a length of 11 cm and a breadth of 8 cm. What is its area?
items.e: Area = length × breadth = 11 × 8. 10 × 8 = 80 and 1 × 8 = 8. 80 + 8 = 88 cm².

items.q: A rectangle has a length of 15 m and a breadth of 4 m. What is its area?
items.e: Area = length × breadth = 15 × 4. 10 × 4 = 40 and 5 × 4 = 20. 40 + 20 = 60 m².

items.q: This is a square. What is its area?
items.e: All sides of a square are equal, so the length and the breadth are both 9 cm. 9 × 9 = 81 cm². (36 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area = length × breadth = 7 × 5 = 35 cm². (24 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: Chloe has 60 cm of ribbon. She sticks ribbon round the edge of a card 15 cm long and 10 cm wide. How much ribbon is left?
items.e: Perimeter of the card: 15 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 50 cm. Left: 60 − 50 = 10 cm.

items.q: Mr Tan puts a fence round his rectangular garden. The garden is 9 m long and 6 m wide. He leaves a gap of 2 m for a gate. How much fence does he need?
items.e: Perimeter: 9 + 6 + 9 + 6 = 30 m. The gate has no fence: 30 − 2 = 28 m.

items.q: Hafiz lays 1 m² tiles only round the edge of a patio 6 m long and 4 m wide, as shown. How many tiles does he use?
items.e: Top and bottom rows: 6 + 6 = 12 tiles. Each side has 2 more tiles between the corners: 2 + 2 = 4. 12 + 4 = 16 tiles. (20 counts the 4 corner tiles twice. 24 would cover the whole patio.)

items.q: All the angles are right angles. What is the perimeter of this figure?
items.e: Add all 6 sides: 10 + 2 + 7 + 4 + 3 + 6 = 32 m. Tick each side as you add it so you do not miss one.

items.q: All the angles are right angles. What is the perimeter of this figure?
items.e: Find the two sides with no label first. The one that goes across: 10 − 4 = 6 cm. The one that goes up and down: 8 − 3 = 5 cm. Perimeter: 10 + 3 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 8 = 36 cm.

items.q: A square garden has sides of 7 m. Fencing costs $9 for each metre. How much does it cost to fence the whole garden?
items.e: Perimeter: 4 × 7 = 28 m. Cost: 28 × $9 = $252. ($441 uses the area, 7 × 7 = 49, instead of the perimeter. $63 pays for only one side.)

items.q: Mdm Wong covers her kitchen floor with square tiles. Each tile is 1 m². The floor is 4 m long and 3 m wide. How many tiles does she need?
items.e: Tiles cover the surface, so find the area: 4 × 3 = 12 m². Each tile is 1 m², so she needs 12 tiles. (14 is the perimeter.)

items.q: Xin Yi makes a rectangle with 12 square tiles: 6 tiles long and 2 tiles wide. Zhi Hao makes a rectangle with 12 tiles: 4 tiles long and 3 tiles wide. Each tile has sides of 1 cm. Whose rectangle has the longer perimeter?
items.e: Both have an area of 12 cm². Xin Yi: 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16 cm. Zhi Hao: 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 cm. 16 − 14 = 2 cm, so Xin Yi’s is longer by 2 cm.

items.q: Siti’s bedroom floor is 5 m long and 4 m wide. A carpet costs $8 for each square metre. How much does a carpet for the whole floor cost?
items.e: Carpet covers the floor, so find the area: 5 × 4 = 20 m². Cost: 20 × $8 = $160. ($144 uses the perimeter, 18 m, instead of the area.)

items.q: During Sports Day practice, Ryan runs round a rectangular field 2 times. The field is 80 m long and 50 m wide. How far does he run?
items.e: Once round: 80 + 50 + 80 + 50 = 260 m. 2 times round: 260 + 260 = 520 m. (80 × 50 = 4000 is the area of the field, not a distance.)

items.q: All the angles are right angles. What is the perimeter of this figure?
items.e: Find the two sides with no label first. The one that goes across: 9 − 4 = 5 cm. The one that goes up and down: 7 − 4 = 3 cm. Perimeter: 9 + 4 + 5 + 3 + 4 + 7 = 32 cm.

items.q: Raju bends a piece of wire 36 cm long to make a square. How long is each side of the square?
items.e: The square has 4 equal sides. 4 units = 36 cm, so 1 unit = 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm. (6 × 6 = 36 would be an area, but 36 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: Mr Kumar has 50 m of fencing. He fences a rectangular pen 12 m long and 8 m wide. How much fencing is left?
items.e: Fencing used is the perimeter: 12 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 40 m. Left: 50 − 40 = 10 m. (30 m comes from using only 12 + 8 = 20 m.)

items.q: The length of a rectangle is 3 times its breadth. The breadth is 4 cm. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: 1 unit = 4 cm, so the length is 3 units = 3 × 4 = 12 cm. Perimeter: 12 + 4 + 12 + 4 = 32 cm. (16 cm is only one length and one breadth.)

items.q: All the angles are right angles. What is the perimeter of this figure?
items.e: Add all 8 sides: 10 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 + 2 = 38 cm. Tick each side as you add it so you do not miss one.

items.q: Mr Rahman fences a rectangular plot in a community garden. The plot is 8 m long and 5 m wide. One long side is against a wall and needs no fence. How much fence does he need?
